sections.title: Research and Analysis
sections.description: Research and Analysis — asking good questions, choosing sources you can trust, spotting patterns, comparing points of view and giving fair ideas with reasons.

sections.title: Stage 4 skills
sections.description: Evaluation, Reflection, Collaboration and Communication — judging how useful a source is, thinking about your own learning, working well in a team and sharing ideas clearly.

sections.title: Foundations (Stages 1–3)
sections.description: Your earliest Global Perspectives skills from Stages 1 to 3 — asking questions, listening, noticing and sorting, being fair and working kindly with others.

questions.question: Amara wants to do a research project about her school. Which of these is the best research question?
questions.options: What is my teacher's first name? | Do I like my classroom? | Is my school bag blue? | How do children in my school travel to school each day?
questions.correctAnswer: How do children in my school travel to school each day?
questions.explanation: A good research question is worth finding out about and needs answers from many people. The other three can be answered in one second without any research.

questions.question: Which of these is an open question — one that invites a long, interesting answer?
questions.options: Have you ever watched a football match? | Why do you enjoy playing football? | Is football played outside? | Do you like football?
questions.correctAnswer: Why do you enjoy playing football?
questions.explanation: An open question, often starting with why or how, lets people explain their thinking. The other three are closed questions — they can be answered with just yes or no.

questions.question: Omar wants to find out how much water his family uses in one day. What is the best way to find out?
questions.options: Keep a tally every time someone in his family uses water for a whole day | Read a storybook about a fish | Ask his friend at school to guess | Copy the first website he finds without checking it
questions.correctAnswer: Keep a tally every time someone in his family uses water for a whole day
questions.explanation: Watching carefully and keeping a tally gives Omar real information about his own family. Guessing, storybooks and unchecked websites cannot tell him what actually happens at home.

questions.question: Zahra finds two sources about healthy eating: a doctor's website updated this year, and an old poster with no author's name. Which source should she trust more, and why?
questions.options: The poster, because it has brighter colours | The poster, because older things are always truer | Neither one — she should just guess instead | The doctor's website, because it is written by an expert and is up to date
questions.correctAnswer: The doctor's website, because it is written by an expert and is up to date
questions.explanation: A good source is written by someone who knows the subject, and it is recent. When we do not know who made a source or when, we should be careful about trusting it.

questions.question: Karim predicts that most children in his class sleep less than nine hours a night. What should he do to test his prediction?
questions.options: Ask only his best friend | Ask every classmate the same question and count up the answers | Say his prediction is right without checking | Change his prediction to match what he hopes is true
questions.correctAnswer: Ask every classmate the same question and count up the answers
questions.explanation: A prediction is a careful guess that still needs testing. Asking everyone the same question, then counting the answers, shows Karim whether his guess was right or wrong.

questions.question: Layla is writing a questionnaire about reading. Which question is clear and fair?
questions.options: You love reading, don't you? | Why are you so lazy about reading? | Reading is the best hobby ever — do you agree or what? | How many books did you read this month?
questions.correctAnswer: How many books did you read this month?
questions.explanation: A fair questionnaire question is short, clear and does not push people towards one answer. The other questions are pushy or unkind, so people cannot answer them honestly.

questions.question: Musa reads a library book page about recycling for his project. What is the best way to take notes?
questions.options: Write a few short points in his own words | Write down only the page number | Copy the whole page word for word | Write nothing and trust his memory
questions.correctAnswer: Write a few short points in his own words
questions.explanation: Short notes in your own words show you really understood the source. Copying everything wastes time, and writing nothing means the ideas are soon forgotten.

questions.question: Hana asked 30 children to name their favourite fruit. What is the best way to show which fruit was most popular?
questions.options: A list hidden in her drawer | A photo of one apple | A bar chart with one bar for each fruit | A long story about her day
questions.correctAnswer: A bar chart with one bar for each fruit
questions.explanation: A bar chart turns the counts into bars, so everyone can see at a glance which fruit got the most votes. Findings should be shown in a way that is easy to read and share.

questions.question: Idris wants to know how the school library is really used at lunchtime. What is the best way to find out?
questions.options: Ask one friend who never goes to the library | Ask his aunt, who has never visited the library | Visit the library at lunchtime and keep a tally of what he sees | Imagine what probably happens
questions.correctAnswer: Visit the library at lunchtime and keep a tally of what he sees
questions.explanation: Watching, with a tally to record what happens, is a great research method when you want to know what people really do. People who have never been there can only guess.

questions.question: Amara has collected questionnaire answers from her whole class. What is the fair and safe thing to do with them?
questions.options: Change the answers she disagrees with | Keep the answers private and never make fun of anyone's answer | Read out the funniest answers with the children's names | Post the answers online for strangers to see
questions.correctAnswer: Keep the answers private and never make fun of anyone's answer
questions.explanation: Good researchers are kind and fair. People shared their honest answers, so we keep them private, never laugh at them, and never change what people really said.

questions.question: Which of these statements is a fact?
questions.options: Our school has 400 pupils | School lunches are boring | Our school is the best school in the world | Football is more fun than reading
questions.correctAnswer: Our school has 400 pupils
questions.explanation: A fact can be checked and proved — you could count the pupils. The other statements are opinions: they tell you what someone feels, and different people would say different things.

questions.question: Sami says, 'Broccoli is disgusting.' Why is this an opinion and not a fact?
questions.options: Because it says what Sami feels, and it cannot be checked or proved | Because Sami said it out loud | Because it is about food | Because everyone in the world agrees with it
questions.correctAnswer: Because it says what Sami feels, and it cannot be checked or proved
questions.explanation: An opinion tells you how someone feels or what they believe. There is no test that can prove broccoli is disgusting — plenty of people love it!

questions.question: Karim counts pieces of litter in the playground: Monday 4, Tuesday 6, Wednesday 8, Thursday 10. What pattern does he spot?
questions.options: There is no pattern in these numbers | The amount of litter goes down each day | The amount of litter stays exactly the same | The amount of litter goes up each day
questions.correctAnswer: The amount of litter goes up each day
questions.explanation: The numbers rise by two every day: 4, 6, 8, 10. Spotting a pattern like this is the first step — the next step is asking why it is happening.

questions.question: A class survey shows: 18 children walk to school, 8 come by car and 4 cycle. What do these numbers tell us?
questions.options: Coming by car is the cheapest way to travel | Most children in the class walk to school | Nobody in the class walks to school | Cycling is the most popular way to travel
questions.correctAnswer: Most children in the class walk to school
questions.explanation: 18 is more than 8 and 4 added together, so walking is the most common way to travel. The numbers say nothing about cost, so we cannot claim anything about that.

questions.question: A town wants to build shops on a park. The shopkeeper is happy, but the bird-watcher is upset. Why do they see the same plan so differently?
questions.options: Because the change helps what one of them cares about and harms what the other cares about | Because grown-ups always disagree about everything | Because one of them must be lying about the plan | Because the park is too big to build on
questions.correctAnswer: Because the change helps what one of them cares about and harms what the other cares about
questions.explanation: People look at the same issue from different points of view. The shopkeeper cares about customers and the bird-watcher cares about wildlife — both can be honest and still disagree.

questions.question: Zahra is comparing what two groups think about a new bike lane. What should she look for first?
questions.options: Whose poster has the neatest handwriting | Which group has the most members with bikes | Where the two groups agree and where they disagree | Which group talks the loudest
questions.correctAnswer: Where the two groups agree and where they disagree
questions.explanation: Lining up different views side by side and finding the agreements and disagreements is how analysts compare fairly. Loud voices and neat handwriting do not make an idea right.

questions.question: Every morning, cars wait with their engines running outside the school gates, and the air there smells of fumes. Which is the cause and which is the effect?
questions.options: The two things are not connected at all | Both things are causes with no effect | Cause: the fumes in the air; effect: the waiting cars | Cause: the waiting cars with engines running; effect: the fumes in the air
questions.correctAnswer: Cause: the waiting cars with engines running; effect: the fumes in the air
questions.explanation: The cause is the thing that makes something happen, and the effect is what happens because of it. The running engines make the fumes — not the other way round.

questions.question: Layla studies litter on her local beach. How does her local problem connect to the wider world?
questions.options: The sea cleans itself, so there is no connection | Litter from many towns can travel into the sea and affect other places too | Litter only ever matters on her own beach | Other countries do not have any litter
questions.correctAnswer: Litter from many towns can travel into the sea and affect other places too
questions.explanation: Many local problems are part of bigger global ones. Litter washed into the sea can drift far away, so what happens on one beach is connected to beaches everywhere.

questions.question: At lunchtime, the oldest children always take the whole football pitch and nobody else gets a turn. Which idea is the fairest?
questions.options: Give the pitch to the fastest runners forever | Let whoever shouts the loudest decide who plays | Stop everyone from ever playing football again | Make a rota so different groups use the pitch on different days
questions.correctAnswer: Make a rota so different groups use the pitch on different days
questions.explanation: A fair idea gives everyone a share. A rota means every group gets real turns, while the other ideas leave most children with nothing — or punish everybody.

questions.question: Karim thinks the school should sell fruit at break time. Which is the strongest reason he could give?
questions.options: Our class survey showed that most children want a healthy snack at break | Because my cousin likes sweets | Because fruit is an easy word to spell | Because I just really want it to happen
questions.correctAnswer: Our class survey showed that most children want a healthy snack at break
questions.explanation: The strongest reasons rest on evidence. A survey result is something you found out, while the other reasons are just feelings that would not persuade anyone.

questions.question: Nadia is finding out what school lunches cost. Which source is the most useful for her question?
questions.options: A poem about eating breakfast | The school's lunch price list from this term | A cartoon about a talking sandwich | A photo of her own kitchen
questions.correctAnswer: The school's lunch price list from this term
questions.explanation: A useful source is relevant — it actually answers your question. The price list is about exactly what Nadia wants to know; the others are about food but not about cost.

questions.question: A website made by a sweet company says, 'Sweets are a healthy snack for children.' What should Nadia think about this source?
questions.options: Be careful — the company wants to sell sweets, so its idea may be one-sided | Ignore every website ever made | Trust it completely, because it is on the internet | Trust it, because sweets taste nice
questions.correctAnswer: Be careful — the company wants to sell sweets, so its idea may be one-sided
questions.explanation: Good evaluators ask who made a source and why. A company selling sweets gains money if you believe them, so their claim needs checking against sources with nothing to sell.

questions.question: Yusuf's team has just finished a project. Which of these is a good reflection on his own teamwork?
questions.options: The project is finished, so there is nothing to think about | I am never going to work in a team again | I listened well, but next time I want to share my own ideas earlier | Everything that went wrong was my teammates' fault
questions.correctAnswer: I listened well, but next time I want to share my own ideas earlier
questions.explanation: A good reflection names something you did well and something you want to improve. Blaming others or refusing to think back does not help you grow.

questions.question: Yusuf learned that some children walk a very long way to fetch clean water. Which sentence shows his learning changed his thinking?
questions.options: I already knew everything about water before | Water is wet and that is all I learned | It changed nothing, because it happens far away from me | I used to leave the tap running, but now I understand why saving water matters
questions.correctAnswer: I used to leave the tap running, but now I understand why saving water matters
questions.explanation: Reflection means noticing how new learning changes what you think and do. Saying 'I used to think... but now...' shows exactly that change.

questions.question: Layla's team of four children is making a poster together. What is the best way to share the work?
questions.options: Give each person a different job that uses what they do well | Have all four children colour the same corner | Let one person do everything alone | Wait quietly and hope the poster finishes itself
questions.correctAnswer: Give each person a different job that uses what they do well
questions.explanation: Good teams share out the jobs so everyone helps and nothing is left undone. Giving each member a different job that suits them gets the best from the whole team.

questions.question: Layla's team cannot agree on a topic for their project. What should they do?
questions.options: Each secretly make a different project | Let the loudest person choose for everyone | Stop speaking to each other | Listen to every idea, then vote or build one idea from the best parts
questions.correctAnswer: Listen to every idea, then vote or build one idea from the best parts
questions.explanation: Teams can disagree and still work well together. Listening to everyone and then deciding together — by voting or combining ideas — keeps the team fair and moving forward.

questions.question: Idris is giving a short talk to his class. What will make his talk clear and organised?
questions.options: Plan a beginning, a middle and an end, and speak about one thing at a time | Tell jokes about a completely different topic | Say everything as fast as possible | Whisper his facts in a random order
questions.correctAnswer: Plan a beginning, a middle and an end, and speak about one thing at a time
questions.explanation: Clear communication is planned and stays on topic. A beginning, middle and end helps listeners follow, and one idea at a time keeps the talk easy to understand.

questions.question: In a class discussion, a classmate shares an idea. What is the best way for Idris to respond?
questions.options: Look at the ceiling until they stop | Listen carefully, then ask a question about their idea | Interrupt and change the subject | Repeat his own idea again, but louder
questions.correctAnswer: Listen carefully, then ask a question about their idea
questions.explanation: Good discussion partners listen first and then respond to what was actually said. Asking a question shows you heard the idea and want to understand it better.

questions.question: Amina wants to learn something her grandmother knows about the old days. What should she do first?
questions.options: Decide it is not worth finding out | Guess what her grandmother might say | Ask her grandmother a question and listen carefully to the answer | Ask her baby brother instead
questions.correctAnswer: Ask her grandmother a question and listen carefully to the answer
questions.explanation: Families are full of things to learn. Asking a question and really listening is the very first research skill — the person who knows can tell you so much.

questions.question: Omar's class made posters to remind everyone to save water. What makes a poster easy for people to understand?
questions.options: No words and no pictures at all | A secret code that only Omar can read | A big clear picture and a few simple words | Tiny writing squeezed into every space
questions.correctAnswer: A big clear picture and a few simple words
questions.explanation: When you share an idea, keep it clear and simple. A big picture and a few well-chosen words let everyone understand your message in one look.

questions.question: Hana wonders how bread is made. What is the best way to find out?
questions.options: Decide that it does not matter | Ask nobody and just guess | Ask her friend who has never made bread | Ask a baker and look in a book about food
questions.correctAnswer: Ask a baker and look in a book about food
questions.explanation: To find something out, go to people and books that really know. A baker makes bread every day, and a food book can show the steps too.

questions.question: The class counted favourite playtime games: skipping got 10 votes, tag got 6 and hopscotch got 3. Which game is the most popular?
questions.options: Skipping | Tag | They are all exactly the same | Hopscotch
questions.correctAnswer: Skipping
questions.explanation: Counting and comparing the votes shows skipping got the most: 10 is bigger than 6 and 3. Sorting answers like this helps us see what the class really thinks.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: How can we be active and healthy?

questions.question: Why does a playground game need rules that everyone follows?
questions.options: So the game is fair for every player | Because rules are only for grown-ups | So nobody new can ever join in | So the fastest child always wins
questions.correctAnswer: So the game is fair for every player
questions.explanation: Rules are made so everyone gets a fair chance and knows what to do. A game without fair rules quickly stops being fun for most of the players.

questions.question: A new pupil who does not know anyone joins the class. What is the kindest way to work and play with them?
questions.options: Tell them all the games are full | Wait a year before speaking to them | Ignore them until they go away | Invite them to join your game and ask their name
questions.correctAnswer: Invite them to join your game and ask their name
questions.explanation: Working well with others starts with welcoming them. Inviting a new pupil in and learning their name helps them feel they belong — and makes your team stronger too.
